stem: Over a long conversation the agent keeps losing specific details — the customer's ID, exact order number, and a precise postcode. What's the most reliable fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Maintain a persistent structured facts block that's carried forward verbatim (not summarized).
options.rationale: Correct. Progressive summarization loses names, numbers, and exact values on each pass. A persistent facts block is copied forward exactly, so the model can't lose those details.

options.label: B
options.body: Ask the model to 'summarize what we've discussed so far' periodically.
options.rationale: Each summarization pass drops specific details — the exact failure here.

options.label: C
options.body: Rely on a bigger context window to hold everything.
options.rationale: A bigger window delays the problem but details still degrade in long, noisy contexts.

options.label: D
options.body: Re-fetch the details from tools every turn.
options.rationale: Re-fetching helps freshness but is wasteful and doesn't preserve the conversational record; a facts block is the direct fix.

stem: A long exploration task will exceed the context window, and findings must survive a context reset. What's the right mechanism, and why?

options.label: A
options.body: Scratchpad files — external persistence on disk that survives any context reset, re-read at boundaries.
options.rationale: Correct. Conversation history is internal persistence (lost when the window fills); scratchpad files are external persistence that survives resets.

options.label: B
options.body: Keep everything in conversation history so nothing is lost.
options.rationale: History is internal persistence — it's exactly what's lost when the window fills up.

options.label: C
options.body: Summarize findings into the system prompt.
options.rationale: Summaries lose detail and still live in-context, not on disk.

options.label: D
options.body: Increase max_tokens so the context can't overflow.
options.rationale: max_tokens is output length; it doesn't extend the input/context budget or survive a reset.

stem: Which is a reliable trigger for escalating to a human — as opposed to an unreliable exam distractor?

options.label: A
options.body: A policy gap or exception — the policy is silent or ambiguous on the request.
options.rationale: Correct. The three valid triggers: the customer explicitly asks for a human, a policy gap/exception, or the agent can't make meaningful progress.

options.label: B
options.body: A sentiment score crossing a frustration threshold.
options.rationale: Sentiment doesn't track case complexity — a frustrated customer with a resolvable issue shouldn't be auto-escalated.

options.label: C
options.body: The model's self-reported confidence dropping below 0.7.
options.rationale: Self-reported confidence scores are unreliable triggers — they don't track actual complexity.

options.label: D
options.body: The conversation exceeding 20 turns.
options.rationale: Turn count is arbitrary and unrelated to whether a human is genuinely needed.

stem: A customer's very first message is: 'Just connect me to a human, please.' The agent has no context yet. Best action?

options.label: A
options.body: Honor the explicit request and escalate — an explicit ask for a human is a valid trigger, without forcing an investigation first.
options.rationale: Correct. An explicit request for a human is one of the three valid escalation triggers; honor it immediately rather than insisting on investigating first.

options.label: B
options.body: Refuse until you've run get_customer and lookup_order.
options.rationale: Forcing investigation before honoring an explicit human request adds friction and ignores a valid trigger.

options.label: C
options.body: List everything the agent can do to talk them out of it.
options.rationale: Capability-listing at someone asking for a human reads as dismissive.

options.label: D
options.body: Run a sentiment check first to gauge urgency.
options.rationale: Sentiment is an unreliable trigger; the explicit request already settles it.

stem: A customer asks for competitor price-matching. Company policy only addresses adjustments on its own site and is silent on competitors. Is this a policy gap or a violation, and what should the agent do?

options.label: A
options.body: It's a policy gap (policy is silent) — escalate for a human decision.
options.rationale: Correct. A gap means the policy doesn't cover the case → escalate. (A violation, where policy forbids it, means refuse with the policy explanation.)

options.label: B
options.body: It's a violation — refuse and cite the policy.
options.rationale: The policy doesn't forbid it; it's silent. That's a gap, not a violation.

options.label: C
options.body: Approve the match, since nothing forbids it.
options.rationale: A silent policy isn't blanket permission — escalate for a decision rather than inventing policy.

options.label: D
options.body: Ask the customer to interpret the policy.
options.rationale: Resolving a policy gap is a human/business decision, not the customer's.

stem: Monitoring shows a stable 95% overall extraction accuracy, yet users keep reporting errors in a specific field type. What's the right diagnostic approach?

options.label: A
options.body: Stratified validation — break accuracy down per type/category to find the underperforming one.
options.rationale: Correct. Aggregate metrics mask per-type issues: 95% overall can hide a category at 60%. Group by type, compute per-type accuracy, then target the weak category.

options.label: B
options.body: Trust the 95% — the system is reliable overall.
options.rationale: Aggregate accuracy hides category-specific degradation; the complaints are real.

options.label: C
options.body: Randomly sample 5% more outputs across everything.
options.rationale: Undirected random sampling can miss a concentrated category problem; stratify instead.

options.label: D
options.body: Raise the overall accuracy target to 98%.
options.rationale: Chasing a higher aggregate still masks the weak category.

stem: Two sources disagree: Source A (2024 docs) says the context window is 200K tokens; Source B (2023 blog) says 100K. How should synthesis handle this?

options.label: A
options.body: Keep both, annotated with provenance and dates, and let the consumer interpret (here it's a temporal change, not a true conflict).
options.rationale: Correct. Never average or silently pick one. Annotate both with source and date; often the 'conflict' is a change over time the dates reveal.

options.label: B
options.body: Pick the more recent source and drop the other.
options.rationale: Silently choosing recency discards provenance the consumer may need — a classic distractor.

options.label: C
options.body: Average the two numbers to 150K.
options.rationale: Averaging conflicting claims destroys the real information and invents a wrong value.

options.label: D
options.body: Only report a claim if two sources corroborate it.
options.rationale: That drops legitimate single-source facts and still doesn't resolve dated differences.

stem: A subagent partially fails while fetching data. What should its error context include so the next agent (or human) can recover intelligently?

options.label: A
options.body: Failure type, any partial results retrieved, what recovery was already tried, and a suggested next action.
options.rationale: Correct. Structured error context (type + partial results + alternatives tried + suggested action) enables intelligent recovery.

options.label: B
options.body: A generic 'Something went wrong' message.
options.rationale: Generic messages give the next agent nothing to work with.

options.label: C
options.body: Only the raw stack trace.
options.rationale: A stack trace lacks partial results, recovery attempts, and a recommended action.

options.label: D
options.body: Nothing — just return empty so the pipeline proceeds.
options.rationale: Silent empties look like 'no data' and corrupt downstream reasoning.

stem: In production, final reports lose citations because the synthesis step used inline links in prose. What's the durable fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Use structured claim-source mappings ({claim, source, url, date}) that survive synthesis, kept separate from prose.
options.rationale: Correct. Inline links get dropped during summarization; structured mappings survive transformations and preserve attribution end-to-end.

options.label: B
options.body: Add more inline links and hope they survive.
options.rationale: Inline citations in prose are exactly what gets lost during synthesis.

options.label: C
options.body: Re-locate sources after the report is written.
options.rationale: Post-hoc matching is fragile and invites misattribution.

options.label: D
options.body: Have the report generator use semantic similarity to guess sources.
options.rationale: Similarity can attribute the wrong source; keep the model's original structured mapping.
